title: The Tibetan traditions, closed
hook: four schools, the stages, mind training, the bardo

segments.voice: Last week ended in Mongolia, with old monks coming forward to teach again. Your line was it returned. What did you help come back? A new week starts, and today a long stretch of the path closes. Day one thousand three hundred thirty-one.

A Tibetan practitioner finishes a session of practice. Maybe it was prostrations, maybe a mantra, maybe a quiet sit by a butter lamp. Before standing up, there's one more thing. The hands come together, and a few lines are said, offering whatever good came from this practice to every living being, everywhere, without leaving anyone out. Then they get up and put the kettle on. It takes less than a minute. And it is a good place to stand while looking back over this whole stretch of the path, because nearly everything we've met in the Tibetan traditions leans toward that one gesture.
screen: `A SESSION ENDS.` → `HANDS TOGETHER.` → `OFFERED TO EVERY BEING.`

segments.voice: First, the schools. Nyingma, the ancient one, tracing back to Padmasambhava and his hidden treasures. Kagyu, the line of Tilopa, Naropa, Marpa and Milarepa, with its long retreats and its songs. Sakya, the school of the gray earth, teaching that the path and its fruit are joined. Gelug, the school of Tsongkhapa, with its great monasteries, its debates and its geshes, and now its geshemas. Beside them, Jonang, the Rime movement that gathered teachings from many lineages, and Bon, Tibet's other tradition, with its own teachers and not a Buddhist school. Second, the stages. The lamrim walked us step by step: a precious human life, death, karma, refuge, all beings as our mothers, and finally calm and insight. Third, mind training. Atisha's teaching, set out by Chekawa in seven points: sending and taking on the breath, bad circumstances as the path, the five strengths, two witnesses. Fourth, the bardo. Death and the in-between, the clear light, the peaceful and wrathful visions recognized as the mind's own display, and a book read aloud beside the dying. Around all of it: butter lamps, mani stones, thangkas painted by rule, the Kalachakra's sand swept away, tulkus returning, and the mountains from Ladakh to Mongolia. Different schools, different emphases. But each, in its own words, sets this practice inside bodhicitta: the wish to wake up for the sake of all beings. That's why a session ends with the dedication. Whatever was done was never only for oneself.
screen: `FOUR SCHOOLS, AND THEIR NEIGHBORS.` · `THE STAGES OF THE PATH.` · `MIND TRAINING IN SEVEN POINTS.` · `THE BARDO AND THE CLEAR LIGHT.` · then, large: `FOR ALL BEINGS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: sit with bodhicitta. Settle, and let the breath find its own pace. Bring to mind someone you love, and wish them well. Then someone you barely know, a face from the street or the store, and wish them well too. Then someone difficult. Then let the circle widen, past your town, past every border, to every being that breathes. When the bell is close, let whatever good came from this sit go out to all of them, the way the practitioner did before putting the kettle on. If you pray, you can use a dedication from your own tradition. The bell holds the time.
The Tibetan traditions. Four schools and their neighbors, the stages, mind training and the bardo, all held inside the wish to wake up for all beings. Today's word.

Your line: for all beings. Today, when you finish something good, a meal, a kindness, a piece of work, pause for one breath and let it be for everyone. Tomorrow the path turns to other schools, starting in China. Day one thousand three hundred thirty-one.

howItsDone: In Tibetan Buddhist practice, a session traditionally begins by recalling bodhicitta, the wish to awaken for the sake of all beings, and ends by dedicating whatever merit came from it to all beings.

original.note: Sanskrit bodhicitta: bodhi, awakening, and citta, mind or heart. The mind set on awakening for all beings.

trapdoor: what you thought: four sects of Tibetan monks.
what it means: four schools and their neighbors, sharing the stages, mind training and the bardo teachings, all aimed at awakening for all beings.
what a scholar hears: Nyingma, Kagyu, Sakya and Gelug differ in lineage and emphasis, and each frames practice with bodhicitta and the dedication of merit.

notes: Block close: summarizes days 1276–1330 from the outline index. Some of those days have no script yet; the recap follows the index titles and hooks. Confirm nothing is misstated (for example the 'two witnesses' and 'one intention' points of lojong).
'Each sets this practice inside bodhicitta' and the dedication of merit at the end of a session: confirm as fair across the four schools.
Bon is described as its own tradition, not a Buddhist school, as day 1287's index says.
The practice offers a dedication 'from your own tradition' if the listener prays; no new prayer is written.
Original: बोधिचित्त with the standard gloss; confirm.

Editor: the lojong recap now names the five strengths (day 1300) instead of 'one intention from morning to night', which is not a lojong point as taught; Rime 'honored every lineage' softened to 'gathered teachings from many lineages'; the garbled Bon clause ('its own and not a Buddhist school') rephrased.
